title: Chunking
summary: Split a document into passages that search can find without losing the meaning of a rule or exception.
detail:
A chunk is one indexed passage. Its size controls how much text travels together; overlap repeats some text in adjacent chunks to preserve context. Keep headings and source identifiers. Test the same labelled questions with the same number of returned results. Hit rate counts questions with any relevant result; recall measures how much of the labelled relevant evidence was found. A split can separate a rule from its exception or a table from its heading. Inspect the actual passages as well as these scores.

Example: A shed rule says structures under a stated height are exempt, except in a protected area. Keep the exception available beside the rule; a perfectly matched fragment can still support the wrong answer.
failures: A boundary can separate a rule from its exception or a table from its heading. Inspect retrieved passages, not scores alone.

title: Embedding model
summary: Represent text as lists of numbers so search can compare questions with passages that use different wording.
detail:
An embedding model converts text into a vector, a list of numbers used to compare texts. These representations can also support duplicate detection, grouping and classification from labelled examples. Similar vectors can help find paraphrases, but similarity does not prove an answer is supported. Test representative questions, including exact identifiers, against a fixed corpus: the collection of searchable documents. Keep the number of returned results fixed. If you change embedding models, the query and document vectors must remain compatible; this generally requires embedding the document collection again.

Example: “Green bin day” and “recycling collection” may be related. “North ward” and “South ward” can also look similar even though their collection days differ. Evaluate both paraphrases and precise identifiers.

Named examples, not recommendations: sentence-transformers, BGE. Check the selected release and deployment before adoption.
failures: Similarity does not establish factual support. Changing embedding models generally requires compatible query embeddings and a newly embedded corpus.

title: Vector index
summary: Find passages quickly by searching their stored numerical representations.
detail:
A vector index stores passage vectors, the number lists produced by an embedding model. Neighbours are vectors most similar to the query vector. Exact search checks the collection for the closest matches; approximate search uses shortcuts that can miss some. Compare the approximate results with exact search on a sample. Measure capacity and storage for the intended collection size, response time, called latency, and recall: how many expected neighbours are returned. Apply realistic access filters. Recheck the results after changing filters or embedding models.

Example: Compare an approximate index with exact neighbours on the same vectors. A faster index that drops the only authorised source is a regression even if its average latency improves.

Named examples, not recommendations: pgvector, FAISS, Qdrant, Weaviate, Milvus, Chroma. Check the selected release and deployment before adoption.
inputs: Passage metadata, such as source IDs, and access filters
failures: Approximate search can miss neighbours. Filtering and changed embeddings can alter results; verify both before replacing an index.

title: Keyword search
summary: Find passages through words, codes, names and phrases. Keyword search supplies a useful baseline and complements searches based on meaning.
detail:
Use keyword search as a baseline: a simple starting result that later methods must improve on. Tokenisation divides text into searchable units; query processing decides how to use them. These choices affect whether a code or phrase matches. At a fixed result count, measure which questions find relevant evidence and how much of that evidence is found. Inspect questions with different wording before deciding that numerical text representations, or embeddings, are needed.

Example: A resident supplies form code PL-104. Preserve an exact-code baseline: a semantically related form with a different code is not an acceptable match.

Named examples, not recommendations: Apache Lucene, OpenSearch. Check the selected release and deployment before adoption.
outputs: Passages ranked by word or phrase matches
failures: Different wording can hide relevant passages. Tokenisation and query processing affect matches; inspect failures before assuming an embedding model is necessary.

title: Hybrid search
summary: Combine exact-word search with search based on numerical text representations to handle both codes and paraphrases.
detail:
Keyword search and vector search each return an ordered list of passages. Hybrid search combines those lists, a step often called fusion. Compare the merged list with each search alone using the same questions and final result count. The extra search adds cost and complexity; it does not guarantee better results. Adjust the blend on development cases, the examples available for design choices, and keep final evaluation cases out of that adjustment.

Example: Merge two rankings of the same passage IDs, then compare at a fixed final result count. Increasing the output from five to fifty is not a fair demonstration that fusion improved ranking.
failures: An extra search adds cost and complexity. Better performance is not automatic; test the blend and avoid tuning against the final evaluation set.

title: Reranker
summary: Rescore a shortlist using the question and each passage together. Keep the strongest candidates for the answer model after this second pass.
detail:
A reranker receives passages already found by search and compares each one with the question. It then changes their order. Compare results before and after this step at the same final result count, and record the extra response time. A relevance score need not be a probability, and scores from different models may use different scales. Text cut off before scoring and relevant passages missing from the first search can still limit the result.

Example: Retrieve fifty candidates, rerank them, and give the writer five. If the right source never entered the fifty, the reranker cannot recover it. Count that retrieval miss separately.

Named examples, not recommendations: BGE reranker. Check the selected release and deployment before adoption.
inputs: Passages returned by the first search
outputs: Passages reordered by a second relevance check
failures: Scores need not be probabilities or comparable between models. Truncated passages and missing candidates can still limit the result.

title: Large language model
summary: Use a language model to draft text, fill defined fields or propose an operation for the application to check.
detail:
A large language model (LLM) generates output from a prompt: instructions and any supplied context, such as source passages. A tool call is a proposed operation with arguments; the application decides whether to execute it. Test the model on an evaluation set of representative tasks. Check required facts, support from sources, appropriate refusals, cost and response time across repeated runs. Fluent output can still be wrong. Model settings do not replace evidence checks or permission controls.

Example: The source says Monday, but the model writes Friday with a plausible citation. Fluent prose and a valid source ID are insufficient; check the stated day against the passage.

Model-family examples: Mistral, Qwen and Gemma. Software that runs model inference, meaning generation from a trained model, includes llama.cpp and Ollama. These are different roles, not recommendations. Check the selected release and deployment before adoption.
failures: Fluent output can contain unsupported claims. Model choice and settings do not replace evidence checks or controls around tool execution.

title: Language-model judge
summary: Use a model to assess an answer against written scoring rules, while keeping its decisions open to review.
detail:
A rubric states what earns each score and how to handle missing or unsupported information. Ask the judge for separate decisions and reasons. Compare these with labels assigned by independent human reviewers, then repeat some cases to check consistency. Calibrating the judge means checking and adjusting its use of the rubric on development cases. Keep that work separate from final evaluation. Agreement is not proof of correctness: answer order, length or a model’s preferences can bias both scores and reasons.

Example: Ask two reviewers to score a sample before calibrating the judge. Inspect cases where the judge rewards a longer answer that adds unsupported facts. A repeatable judge may repeat the same bias.
failures: Agreement is not proof of correctness. Position, answer length and model preferences can bias judgements; keep calibration separate from final evaluation.

title: Classifier
summary: Route questions into defined categories, such as topic, answerability or difficulty. Implement the decision with rules, a trained classifier or a prompted model.
detail:
A classifier chooses a label for an input. An answerability label, for example, says whether the available evidence can answer a question. If a score determines the choice, the threshold is the cutoff for accepting a label. A confusion matrix counts correct and incorrect predictions for each actual class. Use it to inspect missed cases and false alarms separately. Choose the cutoff with the cost of both errors in mind. A high overall score can conceal failures in a rare class; uncertain cases may need review.

Example: An answerability classifier accepts all questions and appears accurate when most are answerable. Its false-positive rate on unanswerable questions is still 100%; report each outcome.

Named examples, not recommendations: scikit-learn. Check the selected release and deployment before adoption.
inputs: The question or measured properties used to classify it
Label meanings and the score cutoff
failures: A high overall score can conceal failures in rare classes. Monitor changing questions and review uncertain cases rather than assuming every route fits.

title: Support checker
summary: Compare answer claims with retrieved evidence and flag claims that the passages do not support. Keep the distinction between support, contradiction and uncertainty.
detail:
A claim is a factual statement within an answer. Compare each claim with the supplied passage and label it supported, contradicted or unresolved. Test the checker against reviewed human labels, including numbers, tables and different wordings of the same fact. Count missed unsupported claims separately from correct claims rejected by mistake. The checker can misread a condition or lose evidence when text is cut off to fit a limit. Even a supported claim can inherit an error from its source.

Example: “The fee is waived for students” does not support “The fee is waived for everyone.” The checker must retain the condition, not merely recognise similar vocabulary.
failures: A checker can misread evidence or lose it through truncation. A positive result does not establish that the underlying source is true.

title: Personal-data detection and moderation
summary: Detect personal data or harmful content at input and output boundaries. Combine appropriate fixed patterns with model checks where needed.
detail:
Personal data includes information that identifies a person; PII is a common abbreviation for personally identifiable information. Moderation checks content against a defined harm policy. Specify what the detector should flag, then count missed detections and harmless text removed by mistake using labelled cases. Unusual formats and ambiguous names can cause errors. Check before text leaves for an external service as well as after generation. Redaction means removing or masking text; doing it only in the final answer cannot undo an earlier disclosure.

Example: A resident includes a phone number in a question. If it reaches an external model before output filtering runs, later redaction cannot undo that transfer. Test the input boundary independently.

Named examples, not recommendations: Presidio. Check the selected release and deployment before adoption.
failures: Unusual formats and ambiguous names cause errors. Check before external transfer as well as after generation; output redaction cannot undo an earlier disclosure.

title: Agentic retrieval
summary: Allow a bounded sequence of searches when one query cannot supply enough evidence. The system can revise its query and decide when to stop.
detail:
Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) supplies searched evidence to an answer model. In an agentic version, the model can choose another permitted search after seeing an earlier result. Start with a fixed one-search workflow as the baseline. Compare answer quality, evidence found, search count, response time and cost. Set a maximum number of searches and a clear stop result when evidence is still missing. More searches can repeat the same mistake rather than improve the answer.

Example: The first search finds the waste policy but not the holiday calendar. A second targeted search can help. Repeating the same empty query ten times adds cost without evidence.
inputs: Permitted search tools and stopping policy
failures: More searches can repeat the same mistake or never reach an answer. Set explicit stopping conditions and inspect unsuccessful search sequences.

title: Corrective retrieval
summary: Check the quality of retrieved evidence before generation. Route weak results to a defined fallback, such as rewriting the query and searching again.
detail:
In retrieval-augmented generation, the answer model receives passages found by search. A corrective workflow first checks whether those passages are useful. A fallback is a defined alternative, such as rewriting the query and searching again. Compare the whole workflow with the original search on the same cases. Check both useful passages rejected by mistake and weak passages incorrectly accepted. The alternative route must obey the same access permissions, and its extra response time and cost count in the comparison.

Example: A check rejects an irrelevant planning passage and searches again for the collection calendar. Test whether the fallback improves the answer, and whether the check incorrectly rejects a useful passage.
failures: The checker can reject useful evidence or accept weak passages. A fallback needs its own evaluation and must respect the original data-access boundary.

title: Self-RAG
summary: Use a model's retrieval and support assessments to guide whether it searches and whether its answer follows the evidence. Treat these as signals to evaluate.
detail:
Self-RAG uses model-generated assessments to guide retrieval and judge whether an answer follows the evidence. Treat those assessments as predictions to test, not independent approval. Compare search decisions and answer support with reviewed labels, then compare the complete workflow with one that lacks those signals. The published trained method uses a specific model and training approach. A general instruction to check an answer does not reproduce that method, and a model can endorse its own mistake.

Example: A generated reflection says an answer is supported, but the source gives a different date. Keep independent labelled checks. A generic “check your work” prompt is not the trained Self-RAG method.
inputs: A compatible model or defined self-check workflow
failures: A model can approve its own mistake. Implementations differ; do not assume a generic self-check reproduces a particular trained Self-RAG method.

title: Adaptive retrieval
summary: Choose a retrieval path according to the question's assessed difficulty. Simple questions may use a short path; complex questions may require several searches.
detail:
An adaptive retrieval workflow first chooses how much search a question needs. One route may use a single lookup; another may gather several sources before generating an answer. Compare correctness, response time and cost for each route against a workflow that always uses the longer path. Inspect difficult questions incorrectly sent to the short route, where necessary evidence may be missing. The saving depends on how often each type of question occurs in actual use.

Example: A simple bin-day query takes one search; a holiday exception may need two sources. Test the cases misrouted to the short path and compare with always using the longer path.
failures: Routing a difficult question to a short path can remove necessary evidence. The claimed saving depends on the actual mix of questions.

title: GraphRAG
summary: Use entities, relationships or graph summaries to retrieve evidence across documents. Consider the approach when questions depend on connections that passage matching misses.
detail:
A graph represents named things, or entities, as nodes and their relationships as links. GraphRAG uses these relationships or summaries of connected groups to find evidence across documents. It may help questions that join facts about several departments or events. First compare it with ordinary passage search on those questions. Include the work to build and update the graph. An extraction error can create a false link; an old group summary can preserve a removed relationship. Keep every claim traceable to its source.

Example: A question asks how several departments share responsibility. Preserve links from each graph claim to its source. A stale summary can repeat a relationship removed from the current policy.
outputs: Related source facts or summaries of connected groups
failures: Extraction errors can create false relationships. Summaries of connected groups can remain outdated after source changes; keep links to the underlying documents.

sources.title: From Local to Global: Graph RAG

title: Late chunking
summary: Let a passage’s numerical representation use surrounding text, including headings that explain what the passage means.
detail:
With ordinary chunking, an embedding model may process each passage separately. With late chunking, a compatible model first processes a larger text and produces representations for its individual text pieces, or tokens. Those representations are then combined within the chosen passage boundaries. Compare retrieval with and without this approach on identical questions. Check that the model exposes the needed outputs and that the larger text fits its context limit. More surrounding text does not guarantee that a chunk preserves the necessary meaning.

Example: A passage says “this exemption” after a heading defines its scope. Compare embeddings made with and without surrounding context, using the same source and questions.
failures: The method depends on compatible model outputs and context limits. Processing a larger context does not guarantee that every chunk retains the needed information.

title: Contextual retrieval
summary: Add a short description of a passage's document context before indexing it for keyword and vector search. Keep the original passage and source relationship.
detail:
A short passage may omit the document name or subject that makes it understandable. Add a brief description of that context before creating its keyword and vector search entries. Keep the original passage separately so a reviewer can distinguish source text from the added description. Compare search results with the unchanged-passage baseline. Generating descriptions adds cost, and a wrong description can mislead both searches. Review examples and update descriptions when their source context changes.

Example: Add that a passage belongs to the North ward calendar. If the generated note says South ward instead, both keyword and vector retrieval can be misled. Keep the original passage separately.
failures: An invented or misleading description can distort both searches. Review a sample and regenerate descriptions when the source context changes.

title: Multi-vector retrieval
summary: Compare smaller parts of a question and passage when a single numerical summary loses important words or codes.
detail:
A vector is a list of numbers representing text. A multi-vector method can keep one representation for each token, a piece of text, rather than one for the whole passage. Late interaction compares these smaller representations at search time. Compare its results with a single-vector baseline on the same questions. Measure storage, indexing work and response time too. Strong matches for individual terms still do not prove that a passage contains the full answer or supports its claims.

Example: A short form code matters more than the paragraph’s general topic. Multiple vectors can preserve local matches, but measure storage and latency alongside retrieval quality.
failures: Additional vectors increase resource use. Matching individual terms still does not establish that the passage contains the complete answer or supports its claims.

title: HyDE
summary: Use a made-up answer as a search aid when the user’s wording differs from the source documents.
detail:
HyDE means Hypothetical Document Embeddings. The model writes a possible answer, converts it to a numerical text representation, or embedding, and uses that to search real documents. Compare this with searching from the original question’s embedding. The hypothetical text is a query aid, not a source. Invented details can steer search toward the wrong passage. Only retrieved sources that pass the task’s evidence checks should support the final answer.

Example: A hypothetical answer helps translate a vague query into likely document language. If it invents Friday as the collection day, do not present that generated text as evidence.
failures: Invented details can steer retrieval in the wrong direction. Only retrieved, checked sources should support the eventual answer.

title: Query rewriting
summary: Rewrite, expand or split a question before retrieval. Preserve the user's original intent and combine results from any necessary subquestions.
detail:
A query is the text sent to search. Rewrite it to express the same need in document language, or split a compound question into separate searches. Compare the evidence and final answer with those from the unchanged question. Count the additional searches, response time and cost. Check that every part of the original request survives: a rewrite can introduce assumptions, and splitting a simple question can add work without useful evidence.

Example: Split “When is collection and what if I miss it?” into two searches. Preserve both requests; a rewrite that answers only the collection day is incomplete.
inputs: Rules for rewriting or splitting the question
failures: A rewrite can alter the meaning or introduce assumptions. Splitting a simple question can add work without supplying useful evidence.

sources.title: Query Rewriting for Retrieval-Augmented Large Language Models

title: Parent-document retrieval
summary: Search small passages, then supply their larger parent sections to the answer model. Retain explicit links between each indexed passage and its parent.
detail:
The indexed child is a short passage used to find a match. Its parent is the larger section supplied to the answer model after that match. Keep a stable identifier linking the two. Check whether the added section contains the necessary rule, condition or exception. A model’s context limit is the amount of text it can process at once. A large parent can use that space and displace other evidence, so compare the benefit with the extra text and distraction.

Example: Search a short shed-height rule, then provide its full section with the protected-area exception. Check that the parent does not consume all context and hide other required evidence.
failures: Larger sections consume context space and can displace other evidence. Check that useful neighbouring information outweighs the extra text and distraction.

title: Semantic cache
summary: Reuse a previous result when a new question is sufficiently similar in meaning. Scope reuse to the relevant source versions and permitted audience.
detail:
A cache stores a previous computation for reuse. A semantic cache accepts a question that is similar in meaning, even when its text differs. That match predicts that the old answer still applies; it is not proof. Check the permitted audience and source revisions before reuse. Compare with fresh execution and count wrong matches as well as extra cache hits. Include nearly identical questions whose correct answers differ, such as two wards with different collection days.

Example: “North ward green bin” and “South ward green bin” are similar strings with different answers. A cache hit is a prediction that needs evaluation, not evidence of equivalence.
failures: Similarity is not equivalence. A wrong match can serve stale or inappropriate information; evaluate the reuse decision as its own classifier.

title: Model size
summary: Compare models of different sizes and capabilities for the same task. Route between models only when a simpler single-model baseline cannot meet the trade-off.
detail:
Model size often refers to parameter count: how many numerical values the model uses to generate output. Size alone does not determine task quality or the cost of a deployment. Compare candidate models on the same question groups, including exceptions, with measured response time and cost. A router chooses which model receives each request and can introduce its own errors. Use one model as a baseline before adding that extra decision.

Example: A smaller model may pass simple extraction but fail on exceptions. Compare task groups and actual deployment cost; parameter count alone does not determine either suitability or price.
outputs: Measured model choice or routing policy
failures: A smaller model is not automatically cheaper or adequate in a particular deployment. A routing error can send a difficult task to an unsuitable model.

title: Caching
summary: Reuse embeddings, retrieval results or answers instead of recomputing identical work. Define which inputs and versions make an existing result valid.
detail:
A cache stores a result so the application can reuse it. Its key identifies the inputs and versions for which that result is valid. Invalidation makes a stored result ineligible after a relevant change. Measure avoided calls and response-time savings, then compare reused results with fresh ones. Test source and prompt updates. A key that omits permission scope or a source revision can return another user’s data or an outdated answer.

Example: The calendar changes but the question stays the same. An answer cache keyed only by question serves yesterday’s rule. Include the source version and access scope in the reuse policy.
failures: An incomplete cache key can preserve stale answers or cross access boundaries. Include relevant model, document, prompt and permission context in the reuse policy.

title: Batching
summary: Process multiple identified requests together and check that every request has the right result.
detail:
A provider batch is submitted for later processing; a local inference batch lets a model process several requests together. Their scheduling, prices and waiting times differ. Measure completed outputs, cost and total elapsed time. Match each result to its input identifier, a step called reconciliation. Keep individual errors and missing outputs visible. The same number of inputs and outputs does not prove completeness when one result may be duplicated and another absent.

Example: A batch sends 100 requests and returns 100 rows, but one request is duplicated and another missing. Reconcile identifiers, not only totals, before treating the run as complete.
failures: Discounts and latency vary by service. Partial failures, limits and missing outputs need explicit handling; matching totals alone cannot detect duplicated or mismatched results.

sources.title: Claude Message Batches: asynchronous processing and result IDs

title: Local models
summary: Run a model on infrastructure you control, then check the hardware, quality and complete data path.
detail:
Inference is the use of a trained model to generate a result. A runtime is the software that loads the model and performs that computation. Compare task quality, response time and resource use on the intended hardware with the existing deployment. Test the actual model precision and memory limits; compressed weights can change results. A locally running model does not make every surrounding tool or telemetry connection local. Inspect where requests, logs and other recorded data go.

Example: A model runs locally but a surrounding tool exports logs. Inspect the full data path; local inference describes where computation occurs, not every connection made by the application.

Named examples, not recommendations: llama.cpp, Ollama. Check the selected release and deployment before adoption.
inputs: Model weights and the software that runs them
failures: Compression and memory limits can affect results. Local inference alone does not establish that every surrounding tool, log or telemetry path remains local.

title: Orchestration framework
summary: Connect the steps of a task and make their order, data and failure behavior explicit.
detail:
An orchestration framework helps connect document extraction, search, generation and checks into a workflow. Test what each step receives and returns, and inspect how failures change the next step. Include the effort to reproduce and modify a failed run when comparing approaches. Framework defaults can hide retries or other behavior. Start by writing down the required sequence; then ask whether a framework makes that sequence easier to maintain than ordinary functions.

Example: A framework retries a failed action automatically. Confirm that the action is safe to repeat rather than assuming retries are harmless because the orchestration library provides them.

Named examples, not recommendations: LangChain, DSPy. Check the selected release and deployment before adoption.
outputs: An executed workflow with visible steps and state changes
failures: Framework defaults can hide behaviour or constrain an unusual workflow. Keep task logic and evidence visible rather than relying on the framework name.

title: Structured output
summary: Request answers in a defined schema for downstream code. Use supported constraints or validation with a bounded correction strategy.
detail:
JSON is a structured text format for exchanging values. A schema defines fields and their allowed types, such as a string answer, a list of citations and a boolean answerable flag. Structured output helps downstream software read those fields reliably. Check how often the first response matches the schema and how often a correction attempt is needed. Limit those attempts. Separately check whether the field values are true and supported: correct JSON structure does not establish correct content. Constraint support varies between models and tools.

Example: An answer has the correct string, list and boolean types but says Friday instead of Monday. Shape validation can pass while the answer is wrong; check semantics separately.

Named examples, not recommendations: Outlines, Instructor. Check the selected release and deployment before adoption.
inputs: Schema defining the JSON fields and allowed values
outputs: Validated fields or explicit validation failure
failures: A valid structure can contain false values. Constraint support varies, and retries add cost without guaranteeing that the facts improve.

code.text:
from pydantic import BaseModel, ConfigDict

class Answer(BaseModel):
    model_config = ConfigDict(strict=True, extra='forbid')
    answer: str
    citations: list[str]
    answerable: bool

def validate_citations(answer, supplied_ids):
    if answer.answerable and not answer.citations:
        raise ValueError('An answer needs a source.')
    if not set(answer.citations) <= supplied_ids:
        raise ValueError('The answer cites an unsupplied source.')

answer = Answer(answer="Friday", citations=["north"], answerable=True)
validate_citations(answer, {"north"})
# The shape and source ID pass; the source could still say Monday.
code.source: Tools of the Trade workshop: standalone local example, no model call

title: Document parsing
summary: Extract text and structure from PDFs, scans, slides and tables before indexing. Preserve page references, reading order and heading relationships.
detail:
Parsing extracts text and document structure from a file. Optical character recognition (OCR) reads characters from scanned images. Compare sample outputs with the original pages, including table values, headings, reading order and page references. Text that looks fluent can still contain an OCR error or a value assigned to the wrong row. Check these inputs before blaming search or answer generation for a downstream mistake.

Example: A two-column calendar is read across rows and assigns Thursday to the wrong ward. Inspect the extracted values and page positions before blaming retrieval or generation.

Named examples, not recommendations: Unstructured, Docling. Check the selected release and deployment before adoption.
failures: Confident extraction can still be wrong. Missing layout or OCR errors can become retrieval and answer failures later.

title: Evaluation framework
summary: Run versioned datasets and scorers through a repeatable evaluation workflow. Use reports and gates to compare changes and identify regressions.
detail:
An evaluation framework runs test cases and applies scorers, the rules or models that assess each result. A gate uses those results to decide whether a change may proceed. Check scorers against reviewed cases before trusting the gate. Require an output or explicit error for every input, and insert a known defect to prove the intended check fails. A built-in metric may measure a different property from the user’s task. Record the metric definition and release threshold.

Example: A runner reports a high average after silently skipping failed cases. Require one visible result per input case, including errors, and prove a known defect makes the gate fail.

Named examples, not recommendations: DeepEval, TruLens. Check the selected release and deployment before adoption.
outputs: Per-case results, summaries and gate decisions
failures: A convenient built-in metric may measure a different property from the one your task needs. Keep metric definitions and release thresholds explicit.

title: Tracing standard
summary: Record connected steps and their timing in a common format. Link retrieved evidence, model activity and outcomes to the version that produced them.
detail:
A trace links the steps of one request. Each recorded step, or span, can contain timing, status and safe references to the evidence or configuration used. Instrumentation is the code that creates these records. Run a known request and check that expected steps and errors appear. Missing steps can hide the cause of failure. Prompts and source passages may contain sensitive data, so define what is collected, who may read it and how long it remains available.

Example: A trace records a generated answer but omits the passages supplied to the writer. You cannot distinguish a retrieval miss from an ignored passage; verify expected fields with a known request.

Named examples, not recommendations: OpenTelemetry. Check the selected release and deployment before adoption.
outputs: Linked spans with versions and outcomes
failures: Missing instrumentation obscures the cause of failure. Captured prompts and passages can contain sensitive data; control access, collection and retention.

title: Wilson interval
summary: Show how uncertain an observed success rate is when it comes from a limited sample.
detail:
A proportion is a count divided by a total, such as 16 correct answers out of 20. A Wilson confidence interval gives a range calculated from that sample. Under its sampling assumptions, a 95% procedure covers the true proportion in approximately 95% of repeated samples. It does not assign a 95% probability to the particular interval you observed. Ask how the questions were selected and whether their outcomes are related before applying the calculation.

Illustrative: 16 correct answers out of 20 gives a Wilson interval of approximately 58% to 92%.
inputs: Total scored cases and confidence level
outputs: A confidence interval for the success proportion
failures: A small or unrepresentative sample can mislead even when the formula is correct.
formula: p̂ = s/n; d = 1 + z²/n; centre = (p̂ + z²/(2n))/d; radius = z√(p̂(1−p̂)/n + z²/(4n²))/d. Interval: centre ± radius. Requires n > 0 and 0 ≤ s ≤ n; use a suitable sampling model.

code.text:
from math import sqrt

def wilson(successes, total, z=1.96):
    if total <= 0 or not 0 <= successes <= total:
        raise ValueError('Use 0 <= successes <= total and total > 0.')
    p = successes / total
    denominator = 1 + z * z / total
    centre = (p + z * z / (2 * total)) / denominator
    radius = z * sqrt(p * (1 - p) / total + z * z / (4 * total * total)) / denominator
    return centre - radius, centre + radius

low, high = wilson(16, 20)
assert abs(low - 0.584) < 0.001
assert abs(high - 0.919) < 0.001
print(round(low, 3), round(high, 3))
code.source: Tools of the Trade workshop: standalone local example, no model call

title: Rule of three
summary: Estimate an upper bound on the failure rate when a test has found no failures.
detail:
If n trials are independent and share the same failure probability, 3/n approximates a one-sided 95% upper confidence bound. One-sided means it supplies an upper limit rather than a lower-and-upper range. Independence means one trial’s outcome does not change the probability of another’s. To apply the result to real requests, the cases must also represent those requests. Zero observed failures is not a guarantee; copies of the same question do not create independent evidence.

Illustrative: zero failures in 60 trials gives an approximate 5% upper bound; the exact binomial bound is 4.87%.
failures: Zero observed failures does not establish zero risk.
formula: For n independent Bernoulli trials with zero failures: approximate 95% upper failure bound = 3/n; exact one-sided bound = 1 − 0.05^(1/n). Assumes a common failure probability.

title: Precision, recall and false-positive rate
summary: Separate wrong acceptances from missed opportunities when a system chooses yes or no.
detail:
For answerability, define positive as a question the evidence can answer. A true positive (TP) is accepted and answerable; a false positive (FP) is accepted but unanswerable. A false negative (FN) is rejected but answerable; a true negative (TN) is rejected and unanswerable. Precision asks how many accepted cases were answerable. Recall asks how many answerable cases were accepted. False-positive rate asks how many unanswerable cases were accepted. Name each denominator, the group being counted, before choosing a score cutoff.

Illustrative: 8 true positives, 4 false positives, 2 false negatives and 6 true negatives give 67% precision, 80% recall and 40% false-positive rate.
failures: The same numerator can produce different claims when the denominator is omitted.
formula: Precision = TP/(TP+FP); recall = TP/(TP+FN); false-positive rate = FP/(FP+TN). A zero denominator is undefined; report it explicitly.

title: Retrieval recall and hit rate
summary: Check whether search found any useful evidence and how much of the required evidence it missed.
detail:
First label which passage identifiers are relevant to each question. The number k is the fixed number of top results you inspect. Recall at k is the fraction of those labelled relevant passages present in the top k results. Hit rate at k counts questions with at least one relevant result. The measures coincide when each question has one relevant passage, but a hit can miss an important exception when several passages are needed. Neither measure proves the final answer used the evidence.

Illustrative: evidence appears for 8 of 10 questions in the top three results, giving an 80% hit rate at three.
inputs: Passage identifiers in the first k search results
Reviewed relevant passage identifiers for each question
outputs: Hit rate at k and mean recall at k
failures: An unlabelled relevant passage can make a valid result appear wrong.
formula: Per query: recall@k = |retrieved@k ∩ relevant| / |relevant|. Hit@k = 1 when the intersection is nonempty, else 0. Average over eligible queries; report queries with no relevant labels separately.

code.text:
def evaluate(cases, search):
    if not cases or any(not case['expected_ids'] for case in cases):
        raise ValueError('Use non-empty, answerable retrieval cases.')
    hits, recalls = [], []
    for case in cases:
        expected = case['expected_ids']
        found = set(search(case['question'], k=2)) & expected
        hits.append(bool(found))
        recalls.append(len(found) / len(expected))
    return {
        'questions': len(cases),
        'hit_rate_at_2': sum(hits) / len(hits),
        'recall_at_2': sum(recalls) / len(recalls),
    }

cases = [{"question": "Which rules apply?", "expected_ids": {"rule", "exception"}}]
result = evaluate(cases, lambda query, k: ["rule"])
assert result["hit_rate_at_2"] == 1.0
assert result["recall_at_2"] == 0.5
print(result)
code.source: Tools of the Trade workshop: standalone local example, no model call

title: Compounding error and independence
summary: Estimate the chance that a whole workflow succeeds when several steps must all work.
detail:
First define success for the complete workflow and for each required stage. Independent stage outcomes do not affect one another; only in that case can you multiply their separate success probabilities. Otherwise use conditional probabilities: the chance a stage succeeds given that the earlier stages succeeded. A recovery step can change what counts as overall success. Measure complete runs rather than treating separately measured stage scores as a guaranteed workflow result.

Illustrative: five independent stages, each succeeding with probability 0.95, all succeed with probability 0.95⁵, or about 77.4%.
inputs: Definitions of success for each required stage
Whole-workflow outcomes or stage outcomes conditional on earlier success
outputs: A workflow success estimate with its assumptions
failures: Multiplying each stage’s separately measured success rate can mislead when stage outcomes are related.

sources.title: Conditional probability and the chain rule

formula: P(A₁ ∩ … ∩ Aₙ) = P(A₁) × P(A₂ | A₁) × … × P(Aₙ | A₁…Aₙ₋₁). Under independence only, this reduces to ∏P(Aᵢ).

title: Run-to-run variation
summary: Repeat the same evaluation to see how much its result changes between runs.
detail:
Keep the cases and settings fixed, then record each run’s score. The range is the smallest to largest observed score. It describes those runs; it is not a significance test, a procedure for assessing a difference under a stated statistical model. A change inside that range is not automatically meaningless. Compare versions on the same cases and assess uncertainty. Repetition cannot repair a question set that excludes important users or failures.

Illustrative: scores of 81, 84, 80, 83 and 82 have a mean of 82 and an observed range of 80–84.
failures: The observed range of repeated scores does not establish whether a difference is statistically meaningful.

title: Agreement between markers: kappa
summary: Measure how consistently two reviewers assign categories, while accounting for how often each category is used.
detail:
Cohen’s kappa compares actual agreement with agreement calculated from each reviewer’s label frequencies: how often they use each category. That expected agreement is a reference calculation, not proof that reviewers guessed. Report the agreement percentage, case count and table of disagreements beside kappa. Results need care when one category is much more common than others or the sample is small. Two reviewers can agree because they share the same mistake.

Illustrative: 85% observed agreement and 65% expected agreement give kappa = (0.85 − 0.65) / (1 − 0.65) = 0.571.
inputs: One label from each reviewer for each case
failures: Agreement can be high while both reviewers repeat the same mistake.
formula: κ = (pₒ − pₑ)/(1 − pₑ), where pₒ is observed agreement and pₑ comes from the reviewers’ label frequencies. Undefined when pₑ = 1.

title: Held-out set
summary: Reserve evaluation cases that do not guide prompt, model or threshold choices.
detail:
Keep some evaluation cases out of decisions about prompts, models and score cutoffs. This held-out set tests how well those choices work beyond the examples used to develop them. If you repeatedly change the system after seeing its results, the set becomes development data. Choose final cases that represent the intended tasks and record changes to the set.

Illustrative: report 96 of 100 on the development set separately from 82 of 100 on an untouched evaluation set.
inputs: Cases not used to choose prompts, models or cutoffs
Rules for when final evaluation cases may be used
failures: Repeated optimisation against the final test makes it a development set.

title: Pinning versions and settings
summary: Keep the relevant versions and settings fixed so a comparison measures the change you intended.
detail: Pinning means identifying a specific revision rather than a name that can silently change. Record the dataset, scoring rules or rubric, prompt instructions, model revision and supported generation settings. Hold them fixed except for the variable you intend to compare. This reduces unexplained differences but does not guarantee identical outputs on repeated runs. Use the settings intended for deployment and record provider changes you cannot control.
outputs: Recorded versions and settings for repeating the comparison
failures: The same recorded settings can still produce different outputs on repeated runs.

title: Digest pin
summary: Detect whether a file’s exact contents changed after its reviewed version was recorded.
detail:
A cryptographic digest, or hash, is a value calculated from a file’s bytes. Record the expected digest after review, then calculate it again when the file is used. A mismatch identifies changed bytes. A match does not prove that the source content was correct or complete. Investigate an intentional update and revise the approval record before accepting its new digest; do not silently overwrite the expected value.

Illustrative: changing one expected fact in an evaluation fixture changes its digest and fails the integrity check.
inputs: Exact bytes of the reviewed file
Digest recorded for that reviewed version
outputs: Match or mismatch with the recorded digest
failures: A hash of incorrect or incomplete data faithfully preserves that error.
formula: digest = SHA-256(exact file bytes). Compare with the approved digest; do not silently replace the expected value when validation fails.

code.text:
from hashlib import sha256

original = b"North ward: Monday"
changed = b"North ward: Friday"
assert sha256(original).hexdigest() != sha256(changed).hexdigest()
print(sha256(original).hexdigest())
code.source: Tools of the Trade workshop: standalone local example, no model call

title: Proving an automatic check can fail
summary: Introduce a controlled defect that the check is meant to detect, confirm the check fails, then restore the correct behaviour.
detail:
Deliberately introduce one defect that the check claims to detect, then confirm the check fails for that reason. A fixture is fixed test data; a gate is a check that decides whether work may proceed. Change a known fixture value or remove required behavior, and verify that the changed path actually runs. Restore the correct behavior afterwards. One detected defect demonstrates this check for this case, not complete protection against every failure.

Illustrative: alter a known result or omit a required output, then confirm the gate reports that specific failure.
inputs: Fixed test data with a known correct result
outputs: Evidence that the intended check can fail
failures: The altered code may not run, or the failure may come from an unrelated error.

title: Bootstrap confidence interval
summary: Estimate uncertainty by repeatedly rebuilding a sample from the observations you already have.
detail:
Bootstrap resampling draws observed units with replacement: an item can appear more than once in a resample. Recalculate the chosen statistic for each resample to get a distribution of possible estimates. For two versions answering the same questions, draw question IDs and keep each question’s A/B results together. For related observations, preserve the relevant groups. Choose an interval method suitable for the statistic and data relationships. Resampling cannot create new independent evidence or repair unrepresentative cases.

Resample question pairs, calculate the mean score difference each time, then construct an interval for that difference. The fraction of resamples favouring B is not itself a confidence interval.
inputs: Observed results paired or grouped to preserve their relationships
The statistic to estimate and the resampling method
outputs: Repeated resampled estimates and a confidence interval
failures: Resampling individual rows can break dependence between cases or paired versions.

title: Power analysis
summary: Plan how much evidence a comparison needs before you collect its results.
detail: Power is the probability that a specified test detects an effect of a stated size when that effect exists. Define the smallest useful improvement, the allowed false-alarm rate, called alpha, and the desired power. Also specify the starting rate or variability, whether versions answer the same cases, and whether cases are related. These assumptions determine the sample-size calculation. There is no universal question count for a five-point improvement. Ask a statistical reviewer to check the design before the run rather than seeking reassuring power afterwards.
inputs: Smallest useful improvement and expected starting rate or variability
False-alarm limit, target detection probability and study design
outputs: Planned sample size under stated assumptions
failures: There is no universal question count for detecting a five-point change.

title: Krippendorff’s alpha
summary: Check agreement when several reviewers score cases, including cases with missing ratings.
detail: Krippendorff’s alpha compares observed disagreement with a reference level of disagreement based on the ratings. Choose a distance rule for the scale: nominal categories have no order; ordinal categories have an order; numerical ratings have measured differences. This rule determines how much two ratings disagree. Alpha can handle several reviewers and missing ratings. Report the scale, case count and uncertainty beside the coefficient. Weighted Cohen’s kappa also handles ordered categories for two reviewers, so graded scores do not rule it out.
inputs: Ratings from the reviewers for each item, including missing ratings
A rule for the size of disagreements on the chosen scale
failures: Treating ordered ratings as unordered categories changes what the agreement score measures.
formula: α = 1 − Dₒ/Dₑ, where Dₒ is observed disagreement and Dₑ is expected disagreement. Define the scale and distance; Dₑ = 0 makes this ratio undefined.

title: Calibration
summary: Check whether predicted probabilities match how often the stated outcome actually happens.
detail:
Define the event first, such as an answer being correct. Among cases assigned about 90% probability, roughly 90% should meet that definition if the probabilities are well calibrated. A calibration curve groups predictions into ranges, or bins, and compares their average probability with the observed fraction of positive outcomes. Report the number of cases and uncertainty for each group. A model saying "90% sure", or assigning a probability to its next text token, does not automatically estimate the correctness of an entire answer.

Illustrative: among 100 answers each assigned 90% correctness probability, 70 are correct. The observed correctness frequency is 70%, with sampling uncertainty.
inputs: Predicted probability for a defined event
failures: A model saying “90% sure” is not automatically reporting a valid probability.
formula: For probability bin B: mean prediction = Σpᵢ/|B|; observed frequency = Σyᵢ/|B|. Report bin sizes and uncertainty; a coarse curve can hide subgroup errors.

title: Drift
summary: Notice when the questions, sources or performance of a deployed system change.
detail: Drift can mean a change in the mix of requests, their content or the relationship between inputs and expected answers. A new mix of task types is a distribution change; more wrong answers is performance degradation. One does not automatically prove the other. Compare defined time windows with the same task-group measures and suitable earlier baselines. Repeating an unchanged test set measures run variation, not whether incoming requests have changed. Ask which users or task groups the monitor might miss.
inputs: Versioned traffic samples and source records
outputs: Evidence of changing data or outcomes
failures: A changed request mix may leave quality unchanged; quality can also worsen without a change in the monitored request mix.

title: Multi-armed bandits
summary: Allocate more requests to options that appear useful while continuing to try alternatives.
detail: A multi-armed bandit treats each option, such as a model configuration, as an arm. A reward is the measured outcome it aims to improve. The policy uses observed rewards to choose later assignments, while exploration keeps some alternatives in use. Record the probability of choosing each assigned option. Because outcomes influence who receives each option, a simple comparison of average rewards can mislead. Use analysis designed for that adaptive assignment. Decide whether your aim is better outcomes during the experiment, a reliable comparison, or both.
inputs: Definition of reward and the rule for choosing an option
Ordered observations with their assignment probabilities
outputs: Changing allocation of requests and estimates that account for the assignment rule
failures: Adaptive assignment is not interchangeable with a fixed randomised comparison.

title: Sequential testing and repeated looks
summary: Plan when an experiment may stop so repeated checks do not create a misleading success.
detail: A fixed-sample test assumes you collect the planned amount of data before making its decision. Rechecking that test after every new result and stopping when it looks favorable can raise the false-positive rate: claiming a difference when the assumed no-difference model holds. Declare the inspection and stopping rule in advance, or use a valid sequential procedure designed for repeated checks. Confidence sequences are interval methods that support repeated inspection under their assumptions; ordinary fixed-sample intervals do not automatically do so.
inputs: An agreed stopping rule or a valid method for repeated checks
outputs: A decision with the repeated-check error rate controlled
failures: Repeatedly inspecting ordinary fixed-sample intervals can inflate false positives.

title: Fair comparisons and causal claims
summary: Check whether the change caused the improvement, rather than merely coinciding with easier cases or different conditions.
detail: Offline, run both versions on the same cases with other settings controlled. These are matched comparisons. In a live experiment, random assignment can help make user groups comparable. Choose an appropriate unit, such as user rather than request, when requests from one person affect each other. An observational comparison uses existing differences without random assignment and needs explicit assumptions about other causes. Even randomisation does not remove measurement errors or interference, where one group’s treatment affects another. Ask what else changed before making a causal claim.
failures: Different traffic or timing can explain the apparent improvement.

title: Consistency across generated answers
summary: Compare repeated answers to identify unstable factual claims or reasoning outcomes.
detail: Compare repeated answers to identify unstable factual claims or reasoning outcomes. Disagreement can guide investigation, but it can also reflect harmless wording or legitimate alternatives. Agreement does not establish truth: a model can repeat the same error. Validate the detection method against independently checked cases.
failures: Consistent repetition can preserve the same false claim.

title: Checking a claim against its source
summary: Separate an answer into claims and assess whether supplied passages support, contradict or leave each claim unresolved.
detail:
Break an answer into individual factual statements, often called atomic claims. For each one, decide whether a supplied passage supports it, contradicts it or leaves it unresolved. This is a check of grounding: the relationship between the answer and its supplied evidence. It does not establish that the source is true or complete. Compare checker decisions with reviewed human labels, especially for numbers, conditions and facts that need surrounding context.

Illustrative: six of eight claims are supported and two are unresolved. The unresolved claims need investigation; their origin cannot be inferred from that result alone.
inputs: Individual factual claims from the answer
Source passages and independently reviewed claim labels
failures: A supported statement can still inherit a false or outdated source.

title: Semantic similarity scoring
summary: Compare generated and reference answers using representations of meaning rather than exact wording.
detail: Text embeddings represent words or passages as vectors, lists of numbers. A similarity measure such as cosine compares those numerical representations and can recognize different wordings of a similar idea. It does not prove factual equivalence or entailment, meaning that one statement supports another. Negation, numbers and missing conditions can change correctness while leaving similarity high. Use compatible representations and check required facts and source support alongside the score.
failures: Sentences with a changed number or an added "not" can still have similar numerical representations.
formula: cosine(a,b) = (a·b)/(‖a‖‖b‖), for nonzero vectors in the same space. Values measure angle-based similarity; zero vectors need explicit handling.

title: Bias and toxicity benchmarks
summary: Use defined test cases to investigate harmful content and differences across relevant groups.
detail: A benchmark is a defined collection of test cases and scoring rules. Start with the harm you want to investigate, such as different refusal rates for otherwise equivalent requests from different groups. Identify what comparison is appropriate in that setting. Report which groups appear in the cases, their case counts and uncertainty in the results. A passing result applies to the measured harm and context; it cannot establish fairness everywhere or replace review of the actual task.
inputs: Relevant test cases and reviewed outcomes
outputs: Scoped evidence about group differences or harm
failures: Passing one benchmark cannot establish universal fairness.

sources.title: Red Teaming Language Models to Reduce Harms

title: Cost and quality trade-offs
summary: Compare cost and quality on the same tasks to identify options worth considering.
detail: Record quality, cost, response time and required safety or capacity limits for each configuration. An option is dominated if another is no more costly and no worse in quality, with at least one strict advantage. The Pareto frontier contains the options not dominated on those chosen measures. Check uncertainty and other constraints before discarding an option. Equal measured scores, called point estimates, do not prove equal underlying quality. Ask which trade-offs are acceptable for the task.
inputs: Quality and cost measured on comparable tasks
failures: The same measured score does not prove that two configurations have equal underlying quality.
formula: A dominates B on cost and quality when cost(A) ≤ cost(B) and quality(A) ≥ quality(B), with at least one strict inequality. Apply only to comparable measures and consider uncertainty and other constraints.

title: Red-teaming
summary: Deliberately try to make the system fail within an agreed test scope, then keep the failures as future checks.
detail: Red-teaming uses adversarial cases: inputs designed to defeat a protection or expose harmful behavior. A threat model states what an attacker can control and what harm matters. Agree which actions the testers may attempt and what counts as a failure. Turn successful attacks into regression cases that must remain fixed after later changes. Continue looking for new attacks. Results from a deliberately difficult or adaptively chosen attack set do not estimate how often ordinary users encounter failure.
inputs: Attacker capabilities, harm to test and permitted actions
Deliberately challenging cases and rules for judging the outcome
failures: The fraction of successful test attacks does not estimate how often ordinary requests fail.

sources.title: Red Teaming Language Models to Reduce Harms

title: Data and evidence
summary: Prepare trustworthy inputs and keep their origins visible.
detail:
Start with the task, who may use each source and how a reviewer can find its original. Parsing extracts text and structure. Chunking splits text into searchable passages. Annotation assigns reviewed labels, such as the expected answer to a question. Training uses examples to change model behavior; evaluation checks behavior against expectations. Keep these uses distinct even when they begin with the same documents. Provenance is the record of where an item came from and how it changed.

Example: a council calendar can be an answer source. Questions written from that calendar become evaluation cases only after their expected answers and source references are reviewed.
failures: Correct text can lose meaning when layout or provenance is discarded.

title: Search and retrieval
summary: Find the evidence needed for a particular question.
detail:
Retrieval finds candidate evidence for a question. Begin with a simple search method and reviewed labels that name which passages are relevant to each question. This first method is the baseline for comparisons. Add keyword matching, vector similarity or a second ranking pass only to address an observed failure. Compare methods at the same final result count. A relevant-looking passage may still be from the wrong ward or revision, and finding correct evidence does not prove the answer used it correctly.

Example: finding a bin calendar for the wrong ward is a relevant-topic match but a task failure.
inputs: Collection of documents the caller may access
failures: A high similarity score can hide the wrong date, ward or policy version.

title: Generation and answers
summary: Turn available context into an answer, structured result or proposed action.
detail:
Generation turns instructions and available context into model output. The prompt is the supplied instruction and context; a structured result uses defined fields instead of free-form prose. Decide what result the user needs before choosing a model. Check output structure separately from source support. A proposed tool call is a request for the application to consider, not an executed action. Record prompt versions and generation settings for comparisons, and return an explicit unresolved result when the permitted evidence cannot settle the task.

Example: valid JSON containing a fabricated collection day is still a failed answer.
failures: Fluent or well-formed output can still be unsupported.

title: Evaluation and decisions
summary: Choose the evidence that tells you whether this system meets its task.
detail:
Evaluation checks whether a system meets a defined task. Start with failures and their consequences, then choose evidence for each part. Search needs reviewed relevant passages. An automated judge needs reviewed scoring decisions. Tools need tests for valid inputs, permissions and actual effects. Hosting needs workload and recovery measurements. A golden dataset is a reviewed set of task examples; it cannot replace all these other checks. Keep every case outcome, missing output and version visible before interpreting an average score.

Keep per-case outcomes, version identifiers, missing outputs and uncertainty visible before interpreting a summary score.
failures: One average score can conceal missing cases and unacceptable failures.

title: Methods and mathematical detail
summary: Understand the calculation, its assumptions and what the number cannot tell you.
detail:
Choose the question before the calculation: correctness, reviewer agreement, uncertainty, comparison, probability calibration or cost. Name the denominator, the total used in a fraction, and the unit of analysis, such as one question or one user. Some methods assume independent observations, whose outcomes do not affect one another. A paired comparison tests both versions on the same units and must preserve those pairs. Ask whether the observations match the method’s assumptions before interpreting its number.

The worked figures are illustrative. Interactive calculations expose arithmetic; they do not validate the dataset or choose an acceptable risk for you.
failures: Correct arithmetic can support the wrong claim when its assumptions do not hold.

title: Build a golden dataset
summary: Create reviewed examples that define the behaviour your project must demonstrate.
detail:
Group the tasks and identify costly failures. Select cases that reflect real use, then add boundary and failure cases; a deliberately failure-heavy set does not represent normal request frequencies. For each case record its ID, question, expected facts or action, relevant source IDs, whether evidence can answer it, reviewer and version. Include missing evidence, conflicts and exceptions. A label is a reviewed judgement of the expected result. A split divides cases into separate groups reserved for different uses. Assign the case’s role: development guides changes, regression catches known failures, and held-out evaluation remains unavailable for design choices.

A golden dataset means reviewed expectations, not a particular split. Mark each case as development, regression or held-out evaluation. Do not repeatedly tune on cases later described as untouched.

Example: North ward asks for green-bin day; source calendar-v3 says Monday. Expected facts include the ward, bin colour and day. A question about an absent holiday schedule should remain unresolved.
inputs: Task groups and questions that represent them
Sources whose authority has been confirmed, and reviewers able to judge the task
outputs: Versioned cases with reviewed expected results
Record of represented tasks and each case’s assigned dataset group
failures: Model-generated expected answers can repeat the system’s own errors.
Closely related cases appear in both development and final evaluation, making the final results look more independent than they are.

code.text:
case = {
    "id": "north-green-day",
    "question": "When is the North ward green bin collected?",
    "required_facts": ["North ward", "green bin", "Monday"],
    "source_ids": ["calendar-v3:north"],
    "answerable": True,
    "split": "development",
}
assert case["source_ids"] and case["required_facts"]
code.source: Tools of the Trade workshop: standalone local example, no model call

title: Write and calibrate the rubric
summary: Make the expected result clear enough that reviewers can disagree usefully.
detail:
A rubric is a written set of scoring rules. Specify required facts or permitted actions, unsupported additions and when a case cannot be scored. Give the same sample to reviewers to label independently. Discuss disagreements and refine the instructions on development cases; this is rubric calibration. Keep the rubric fixed for the comparison. If a model scores answers, compare its labels with the reviewed human decisions before relying on it.

Example: “Names Monday” alone is insufficient if the question also identifies the ward and bin colour. Mark each required fact and any invented exception. Do not quietly change expected facts after seeing a candidate’s result.
failures: Ambiguous labels make apparent system differences impossible to interpret.

title: Separate training, development and test data
summary: Give each example a declared role before using it to improve or measure the system.
detail:
Training examples can change model weights, the numerical values learned by the model, or guide an optimisation procedure. Development examples help choose prompts, score cutoffs and models. Final test examples assess those choices after they are fixed. A regression set checks previously discovered failures and can remain visible during development; it is not automatically an untouched final test. Leakage occurs when information from a final test case influences those earlier choices. Keep related documents, conversations or events together when splitting data.

Split at the unit that prevents leakage: document, user, event or time period where appropriate. Two paraphrases of the same source question in different files do not create independent evidence.
outputs: Checks for overlaps and inappropriate reuse
failures: Tuning repeatedly against the final test makes it a development set.

title: Review synthetic evaluation cases
summary: Use generated candidates to extend coverage, then check their facts and independence.
detail:
Synthetic cases are generated examples rather than observations collected directly from users. Record the source used to create each one, the generator, its instructions, subsequent edits and reviewer. This is the case’s provenance. Check expected answers against independent source evidence, then look for duplicates and related cases across development and final-test sets. A model can draft questions, but putting its answer in a dataset does not make that answer authoritative.

Example: a generator creates ten versions of the same bin-day question. They may test wording variation, but they do not provide ten independent policy scenarios. Report their shared origin and retain real or independently authored evaluation cases.
outputs: Record of each case’s origin and any overlap with other cases
failures: Synthetic cases may preserve the generator’s blind spots or copy training examples.

title: Run a controlled baseline
summary: Measure a known version before claiming that a change helps.
detail:
A baseline is the known version against which you compare a change. Record exact revisions of the system, cases, source collection, prompt, scoring rubric and supported model settings. First run a small pilot with known results, including a deliberate failure. Check that every input ID has an output or explicit error. Then compare alternatives on the same cases and repeat runs when outputs can vary.

Report results for each task group, case counts, response time, cost and missing outputs. Preserve initial failures when a retry succeeds. The later result does not erase evidence that a rule the system must always satisfy was broken.
failures: A skipped case or wrong system version can make an apparent improvement meaningless.

title: Interpret confidence and uncertainty
summary: Distinguish confidence in a prediction from uncertainty in an evaluation result.
detail:
Prediction calibration asks whether events assigned a given probability occur at about that rate. A confidence interval describes uncertainty in a measured statistic using a stated sampling procedure. These answer different questions, and neither is established by a model sounding certain. Repeated runs show variation on the selected cases; they do not make those cases representative of future requests. First ask whether the number describes one prediction, an observed test score or variation between runs.

Example: a classifier reports 90% confidence for one answer while a small test set gives a wide interval for overall accuracy. These are different quantities and must not be merged into a universal readiness score.
inputs: Labels, sample design and repeated results
failures: A precise-looking percentage may hide a small denominator or an invalid sampling assumption.
